opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated aspects of learning from human data. When you look at how a robot policy is typically trained, it sees maybe the last frame or a short window of a few frames, and then it predicts the next action. That works reasonably well for short, reactive tasks, like picking up a block. But human behavior just isn't structured that way.

Humans are fundamentally non-Markovian when you observe them from the outside. If you watch someone in a kitchen, what they do at any given moment depends heavily on what they did a minute ago, or ten minutes ago. Did they already add salt? Did they already check the fridge? Which step of the recipe are they on? None of that is visible in a single snapshot of the scene. The state of the world doesn't fully capture the state of the task, and it certainly doesn't capture the person's intent. So if your model only looks at a short window, it sees two moments that look identical but where the person did completely different things, and from the model's perspective that just looks like noise or multimodality it can't resolve.

The second reason is that human data is messy in a way robot teleoperation data usually isn't. People pause, look around, get distracted, correct mistakes, interleave subtasks. If you want to extract the underlying structure, the goals and the progress toward them, you need enough history to see the pattern. Long context lets the model infer latent variables like intent, task phase, even individual preferences or habits, which are what actually explain the behavior.

Third, there's a memory aspect for the downstream robot. A lot of real-world tasks require remembering things that are no longer in view: where you put an object, what's inside a drawer you closed, how many items you've already packed. If we want robots that learn from humans to do these long-horizon tasks, the policy needs to carry that information forward, and the training data from humans is exactly where those long-range dependencies show up.

Historically the challenge has been that naively feeding in long histories makes models overfit. They latch onto spurious correlations in the past frames, the so-called copycat problem, and data is limited. But with better architectures, more scalable sequence models, and much larger and more diverse human datasets, like egocentric video and wearable capture, I think we're finally at the point where we can exploit long context properly. To me that's one of the key ingredients for going from robots that do short skills to robots that actually understand and carry out tasks the way people do.

r001.rationale: The response explains that actions depend on earlier events and that history helps infer intent, task phase, and progress.

r002.rationale: It says identical-looking moments can lead to different actions and appear as unresolved “noise or multimodality” when the model has too little context.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that human behavior is almost never a reaction to the last second of observation. When you watch a person cook a meal or tidy up a room, what they do next depends on what they did ten minutes ago, what they're trying to accomplish overall, and sometimes on preferences or habits that only show up over a very long horizon. If you train a model on short windows, you're essentially asking it to predict actions from a snapshot, and the snapshot is ambiguous. The same visual state can lead to many different reasonable actions depending on history and intent. So the model ends up averaging over all of those possibilities, and you get behavior that looks hesitant or inconsistent.

Long context is what lets the model resolve that ambiguity. It can see the earlier steps, infer the goal, and keep track of things like which objects have already been handled or what mistakes happened along the way. That matters a lot for recovery and for the multi-stage tasks we actually care about in robotics, where success is defined over minutes, not frames.

The other piece is that human data is noisy and diverse. Different people do the same task in different orders and with different styles. With enough context, the model can pick up on which style it's observing in this particular episode and stay coherent with it, rather than drifting between modes. So in a sense long context is doing some of the work that explicit task specification or hierarchical planning used to do, but learned directly from the data. It's not the whole answer, but I think it's one of the key reasons we're starting to see imitation from human data scale in ways it didn't before.

r001.rationale: The response says a person’s next action depends on their history, goals, and habits, and that context lets the model infer the goal and explain the action.

r002.rationale: It explains that short-window snapshots are ambiguous because the same state can lead to many reasonable actions, so the model averages over those possibilities.

astra-6.text:
I think long context is important because human behavior only makes sense when you understand what led up to it. If you look at a single action, it can be ambiguous. Someone opens a drawer—are they looking for a utensil, putting something away, or checking whether something is there? The action itself doesn’t tell you their goal.

Over a longer sequence, you can see what they’re trying to accomplish, what they’ve already tried, and how they respond when something doesn’t work. That gives you a much richer signal for learning from human data. You’re learning how actions connect to intentions and how those intentions persist or change over time.

And there are multiple timescales. A movement might take a second, but the task it serves might take several minutes. To model that behavior well, you need to connect those levels. Long context gives you the opportunity to do that, although the model still has to learn which parts of the history actually matter.

r001.rationale: The response says actions are ambiguous without the history that led up to them, and that longer sequences reveal goals and intentions.

r002.rationale: It gives several possible interpretations of one action, but does not state that insufficient context makes behavior appear as a broad distribution of possible actions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human behavior only makes sense when you look at it over time. If you see someone reach for a cup, that movement alone doesn’t tell you very much. Are they drinking, cleaning up, or making coffee for someone else? The intent depends on what happened before, and often on a goal that was established much earlier.

So if we want models to learn from human data, we need them to connect those different timescales: the immediate action, the task someone is doing, and the broader goal. With a short context, a model might imitate a movement quite well but miss why that movement was appropriate.

Long context also gives you a chance to learn from how people adapt. People make mistakes, notice something has changed, and revise their plans. That whole sequence is useful information. For robotics, especially, we want a system that can use that history to decide what to do next, rather than treating every observation as a fresh start.

r001.rationale: The response explains that context reveals why a person took an action and connects the action to the task and broader goal.

r002.rationale: It says short context can make a model miss why an action was appropriate, but does not state that insufficient context makes behavior appear as a broad distribution of possible actions.
